https://www.thetimes.com/article/insect-.title: Insect thought to be extinct discovered in Outer Hebrides
https://www.thetimes.com/article/insect-.text:
A rare insect thought to be extinct in Britain has been found alive and well and living in the Outer Hebrides.
The caddisfly Limnephilus pati, once a native of the East Anglian fens, was unrecorded in the UK for more than a century until a male of the species was attracted to a light trap, owned by Robin Sutton, an amateur entomologist on the island of South Uist.
Sutton, who has attracted 23 species of caddisfly to his light trap over the years, said: “I’ve been running a light trap for over four years but I couldn’t believe that the only location for a species thought to be extinct in Britain was in my back garden.
“It goes to show how much we still have to find out about these far-flung places.”
Caddisflies, from the order Trichoptera (meaning “hairy-winged), are often mistaken for moths, which they are closely related to. There are about 200 varieties in the UK, all living close to water. Adults are usually nocturnal and are attracted to light.
Limnephilus pati is rare, associated with only 16 other sites worldwide in Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, the Isle of Man and Poland.
Paul Hetherington, communications director for Buglife, the invertebrate conservation trust, said: “This is by far the farthest north they have ever been found. It could well be climate change that has led them to move northwards.”
South Uist is rich in habitats for caddisflies, with numerous small lochans, clear, low nutrient streams, and extensive machair habitats.
Craig Macadam, Buglife’s conservation director, said: “It is really exciting that this species, thought to be extinct, has been rediscovered in the British Isles. We don’t know a lot about its requirements but the discovery of this new population means that we might be a step closer to working out what has driven the declines of this species elsewhere.
